newsitem.title: USA: US budget deal a longer-term positive for Wall St.
newsitem.headline: US budget deal a longer-term positive for Wall St.

text.p: The capital gains tax cut in the proposed balanced budget deal could release some pent up selling pressure in the U.S. stock market but longer-term the deal is seen as a positive for Wall Street.

Tobacco taxes in the deal are lower than original proposals, providing some relief to tobacco stocks, while aviation taxes and fees were seen potentially raising costs for airliners, particularly international carriers.
Some analysts argued that capital gains tax cuts in the budget pact could boost U.S. merger and acquisition activity, already at a record level.
The agreement announced Monday between congressional leaders and the Clinton administration aims to balance the $1.5 trillion budget by 2002.

While not in itself a major boon for stocks, the deal is a generally positive step toward holding down inflation and interest rates, the backbone to the current roaring bull stock market, market analysts said.

"Longer-term if we can maintain fiscal discipline and actually run some surpluses to knock down the federal deficit, it would definitely be a positive to the whole interest-rate structure," said Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal.
Among proposals are provisions for a cut in the capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from 28 percent and a second drop to 18 percent in 2001 for long-term holdings.
The capital gains cut could bring about some selling by investors who had been holding off unloading shares in anticipation of a lower tax bite, analysts said.
But in the long run it could make investing in stocks more attractive, they said.

"Longer-term it makes investing, especially in smaller-cap, non-dividend-paying equities, a very profitable business relative to ordinary income," said Charles Pradilla, market analyst at Cowen and Co.

The federal tax on cigarettes, currently $0.24 a pack, would rise $0.10 a pack in the year 2000, and then go up another $0.05 in the year 2002. But the tax would be less than some contemplated, including a Senate proposal of a $0.20-a-pack hike.

"One could always argue that no tax is good news, but short of that argument, a lower tax hike is better than a higher tax hike," said Martin Feldman, Smith Barney tobacco industry analyst. Shares in cigarette makers rose on Tuesday aternoon, with Philip Morris Cos Inc up 3/4 to 45-5/8 and RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp up 3/4 to 33.

The deal would gradually scale back the airline ticket tax to 7.5 percent from 10 percent. But the per flight segment tax would rise to $3 from $2, while the international arrival and departure tax would be $12 each way, compared with the current $6 departure tax.
Due to stiff competition, airlines will not likely be able raise fares to completely offset higher taxes, analysts said.
"It's going to hurt, primarily, those carriers with international operations, since it effectively quadruples the international taxes," said Jeff Long, an airline analyst with J.P. Morgan.

Nonetheless, airline shares rose on Tuesday as the package was seen as less severe than earlier proposals. American Airlines parent AMR Corp was up 2-11/16 to 104-11/16 and Delta Air Lines Inc gained 1-15/16 to 87-5/8.
Wall Street merger and acquisition activity could get a boost from the budget deal.
Stephen Blum, a corporate finance partner at KPMG Peat Marwick, said he expected a speed-up in M&A activity involving medium-sized companies valued at less than $100 million.

"Any time you lower the capital gains tax you allow small business owners to turn their businesses into cash with less costs," Blum said. The lower tax rate and the increased number of deals will also eventually lower overall prices in M&A deals, Blum said.
The budget deal could also boost the number of larger deals involving cash instead of stock, he said.
